neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, date, and situation. MMSE 24/30 — lost 1 point on repetition (could not repeat 'No ifs, ands, or buts'), lost 2 points on sentence writing (wrote an incomplete sentence with word substitution errors), lost 2 points on recall (1/3 words at 5 minutes, retrieved 1 additional with category cue), lost 1 point on naming (named 'watch' correctly but called the 'pen' a 'pin'). MoCA 20/30 with deficits in delayed recall (2/5 words, 1 with category cue), sentence repetition (0/2 — could not repeat either sentence accurately), verbal fluency (8 animals in 60 seconds), and naming (2/3 — phonemic paraphasia on 'rhinoceros'). Speech is fluent with frequent word-finding pauses and occasional phonological paraphasias ('aminal' for 'animal', 'hostipal' for 'hospital'). No agrammatism. No apraxia of speech.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Facial expression symmetric. Hearing intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone throughout. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor. No myoclonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Vibration sense intact at great toes bilaterally. Proprioception intact at toes. No cortical sensory deficits.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No frontal release signs.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride length. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp reflex. No alien limb phenomenon. Clock drawing 10/10 — spatially accurate with correct number placement and hand position. Cube copy intact. Luria hand sequence performed correctly. Praxis testing: able to pantomime tool use without difficulty. Ideomotor apraxia absent.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive difficulty finding words and following conversations
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. James Washington is a 62-year-old right-handed retired high school English teacher who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of progressive word-finding difficulty over the past two years. His wife, who accompanies him, first noticed that he began having frequent pauses mid-sentence while teaching, searching for common words that he would previously have used effortlessly. He would often substitute a related but incorrect word or produce phonological errors such as saying 'aminal' for 'animal' or 'hostipal' for 'hospital.' His students and colleagues began to notice these difficulties during his final year of teaching. He retired two years ago, and while he initially attributed his language problems to stress and burnout, the difficulties have continued to worsen. His wife reports that he now frequently loses his train of thought mid-sentence and cannot repeat back sentences longer than about five words. He struggles to follow complex conversations, especially in group settings, and has difficulty understanding sentences with complex syntax, though he can understand individual words and short phrases without trouble. He has particular difficulty with phone conversations where he cannot rely on visual context. Despite these language deficits, his episodic memory remains remarkably intact. He remembers appointments, recent conversations (even if he struggles to articulate his thoughts), recent news events, and daily routines without difficulty. He has not gotten lost, does not repeat questions, and manages his medications independently. His wife notes no personality changes, no behavioral disinhibition, and no significant executive dysfunction beyond the language impairment. He continues to manage their household finances and performs daily activities independently apart from avoiding situations requiring extended conversation. He was evaluated by a psychiatrist 6 months ago who diagnosed depression related to retirement and started sertraline 100 mg daily. His mood has improved significantly, but the language difficulties have continued to worsen despite mood improvement, prompting this referral. He denies headaches, seizures, visual changes, weakness, numbness, or swallowing difficulty.

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly linguistic profile. Confrontation naming is markedly impaired (Boston Naming Test 35/60). Sentence repetition is severely impaired in a length-dependent manner (100% for 3-word, 0% for 12-word sentences), indicative of a phonological working memory deficit. Non-word repetition is at the 2nd percentile. Verbal fluency is impaired for both semantic (7 words/min) and phonemic (FAS 18 total) categories. Episodic memory (CVLT-3 long delay recall 10/16, z = −0.5), visuoconstructive skill, and single-word comprehension are preserved. No apraxia of speech identified. Profile is most consistent with a logopenic aphasia syndrome

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia (lvPPA) due to Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: svPPA features impaired single-word comprehension and loss of object knowledge with anterior temporal atrophy; this case shows preserved semantics with phonologic errors and left perisylvian atrophy, more consistent with lvPPA
nfvPPA has effortful, agrammatic speech with apraxia of speech; this case has fluent speech with anomia and phonologic errors typical of lvPPA
FTLD pathology can underlie any PPA variant; lvPPA is typically AD-pathology driven, and positive amyloid PET strongly supports AD over FTLD
Progressive over months to years rather than acute onset; MRI shows atrophy rather than infarct
Structured language testing reveals true anomia and phonologic errors that are not explained by reduced motivation

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Order reversible-cause labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, folate; consider RPR/HIV per risk)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Asymmetric (left-greater-than-right) perisylvian / posterior temporal cortical atrophy

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Phonologic anomia and impaired sentence repetition with preserved single-word comprehension and object knowledge

optimal_actions.action: Order CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau, total tau) for ATN classification
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 (or reduced Aβ42/40 ratio) with elevated p-tau supporting A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order amyloid PET when CSF biomarkers are unavailable or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after clinical assessment and MRI
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention (SUVr above positivity threshold) confirming amyloid pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order FDG-PET to assess regional metabolism and distinguish AD from frontotemporal dementia or other neurodegenerative patterns
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Asymmetric left posterior temporal / temporoparietal hypometabolism

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No clinically significant interactions; counsel on GI side effects and bradycardia risk

optimal_actions.action: Consider targeted early-onset Alzheimer gene panel (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) if family history suggests autosomal-dominant disease
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pathogenic variant only in a minority of early-onset cases with a strong family history; result informs genetic counseling more than acute management

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family, discuss prognosis, advance directives, and driving / safety assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and caregiver engaged in care planning; safety concerns (driving, finances, medication management) addressed

useless_tools.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup
EEG is non-specific in Alzheimer's disease and not part of the routine dementia workup; reserved for suspected seizures, encephalopathy, or rapidly progressive dementia

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
Use FDG-PET to characterize the regional metabolic pattern and distinguish atypical AD from FTD or DLB
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit

In lvPPA, the language phenotype (phonologic anomia, impaired sentence repetition with preserved semantics) is more sensitive than imaging for the syndromic diagnosis; AD is the most common underlying pathology
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Differentiating logopenic variant PPA from other PPA variants and recognizing AD as the underlying pathology in an atypical language-predominant presentation initially attributed to depression
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of lvPPA as an atypical AD variant, the importance of differentiating PPA subtypes, and the role of biomarkers in confirming AD pathology in atypical presentations
key_educational_points: Logopenic variant PPA is the PPA subtype most commonly caused by underlying Alzheimer disease
The triad of word-finding difficulty + phonological paraphasias + impaired sentence repetition with preserved comprehension characterizes lvPPA
Preserved hippocampal volumes do not exclude AD — atypical variants target different cortical regions
Depression can delay diagnosis of neurodegenerative disease when cognitive symptoms are attributed to psychiatric illness
Amyloid biomarkers are essential for confirming AD pathology in atypical presentations
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Atypical language-predominant AD variant, requires FDG-PET (left perisylvian) + amyloid PET to distinguish from semantic/nonfluent PPA
